table.caption: Country E: price level (GDP deflator), real GDP and unemployment (invented data for practice)

adas-short-run-changes-s2.title: A shift in Country F's AD-AS graph

adas-short-run-changes-s3.title: Two shocks at once in Merovia
adas-short-run-changes-s3.text: Merovia is an invented country in long-run equilibrium. In the same quarter, two things happen: a worldwide rise in the price of fuel raises costs for most Merovian firms, and a boom in Merovia's main trading partner raises foreign purchases of Merovian goods.

items.q: Using the table, calculate Country E's inflation rate from Year 2 to Year 3.

mistakes.why: 6 is the change in index points. The inflation rate divides it by the Year 2 index: $\frac{6}{104} \times 100$.
You divided by the Year 3 index. Measure the change from the earlier year, 104.

items.q: Based on the table, which change from Year 1 to Year 2 best fits the data?
options: AD shifted right: the price level and real GDP both rose
SRAS shifted left: the price level rose and real GDP fell
AD shifted left: the price level and real GDP both fell
SRAS shifted right: the price level fell and real GDP rose

why.correct: From Year 1 to Year 2 the price level and output both rose and unemployment fell: a rightward AD shift.
options: Right: both rising together is the mark of a rise in AD, demand-pull inflation.
Real GDP rose from 800 to 840, so this is not a fall in SRAS.
Both rose from Year 1 to Year 2.
The price level rose from 100 to 104, so SRAS did not shift right.

items.q: Based on the table, what most likely happened from Year 2 to Year 3?
options: A positive demand shock: AD shifted right, raising the price level and real GDP
A negative supply shock: SRAS shifted left
A negative demand shock: AD shifted left, lowering the price level and real GDP
A positive supply shock: SRAS shifted right, lowering the price level

why.correct: The price level rose while real GDP fell and unemployment rose: the pattern of a leftward SRAS shift.
options: Real GDP fell from 840 to 820, so AD did not rise.
Right: prices up, output down and unemployment up together is cost-push inflation, stagflation.
The price level rose, which a fall in AD alone would not do.
The price level rose from 104 to 110.

items.q: Based on the table, which shift best explains the change from Year 3 to Year 4?
options: SRAS shifted left: the price level fell and real GDP fell
SRAS shifted right: the price level fell and real GDP fell
AD shifted left: the price level and real GDP both fell
AD shifted right: unemployment rose

why.correct: From Year 3 to Year 4 the price level fell (110 to 108), real GDP fell and unemployment rose: AD shifted left.
options: A leftward SRAS shift raises the price level; here it fell.
A rightward SRAS shift raises real GDP; here it fell.
Right: both falling together, with unemployment rising, is a negative demand shock.
More AD raises output and lowers unemployment.

items.q: According to the graph, what happens to the price level and real GDP after the shift?
options: The price level and real GDP both rise
The price level falls and real GDP rises
The price level and real GDP both fall
The price level rises and real GDP falls

why.correct: The new SRAS crosses AD higher and further left: a higher price level and lower real GDP.
options: Both rise when AD shifts right. Here SRAS shifted left.
That is a rightward SRAS shift, the opposite of the graph.
Both fall when AD shifts left. Here AD did not move.
Right: SRAS moved left along the AD curve, up and to the left.

items.q: What kind of inflation does the graph show?
options: Cost-push inflation
Demand-pull inflation
Disinflation
Deflation

why.correct: A leftward SRAS shift raises the price level while output falls: cost-push inflation.
options: Right: rising costs shifted SRAS left and pushed the price level up.
Demand-pull comes from AD shifting right; AD did not move here.
Disinflation is a slowdown in inflation. Here the price level rises because of a cost increase.
Deflation is a falling price level. Here it rises.

items.q: In the short run, what happens to Country F's unemployment rate after the shift in the graph?
options: It falls, because the price level rises
It rises, as firms need fewer workers to produce less
It stays the same, because AD did not move
It falls, because higher costs force firms to hire more workers

why.correct: Real GDP falls, so firms need fewer workers and unemployment rises: higher prices and higher unemployment together, stagflation.
options: A higher price level here comes with lower output, which cuts jobs.
Right: lower output means fewer jobs, so unemployment rises along with the price level.
Output fell, so employment falls too, whichever curve moved.
Higher costs lead firms to produce less, so they hire fewer workers.

items.q: In Merovia, what is the short-run effect of the two shocks on the price level?
options: It falls
It stays the same, because the shocks cancel
It rises
It depends on the sizes of the two shocks

why.correct: SRAS shifts left and AD shifts right: each alone raises the price level, so together it surely rises.
options: Neither shock lowers the price level; both raise it.
They cancel for output, perhaps, but both push the price level the same way: up.
Right: the fuel shock (SRAS left) and the export boom (AD right) both push the price level up.
The sizes matter for output, not for the price level, which both shocks raise.

items.q: In Merovia, what is the short-run effect of the two shocks on real GDP?
options: It rises, because exports are part of AD
It falls, because higher fuel costs reduce output
It stays the same, because the two effects cancel
It is indeterminate: it depends on which shift is larger

why.correct: One shift pushes output down and the other up, so the net change in real GDP depends on their sizes.
options: The export boom raises output, but the fuel shock lowers it at the same time.
The fuel shock lowers output, but the export boom raises it.
They cancel only if the shifts happen to be equal in effect; without sizes, it is indeterminate.
Right: the fuel shock lowers output and the export boom raises it.

items.q: Show both of Merovia's shocks on the AD-AS graph and mark the new short-run equilibrium.

why.correct: The fuel shock shifts SRAS left and the export boom shifts AD right. The price level rises; the change in real GDP depends on the sizes.

key.because: higher fuel costs and more foreign purchases

items.q: The world price of oil falls sharply. Shift the right curve and mark the new short-run equilibrium.

why.correct: Cheaper oil lowers costs, so SRAS shifts right: the price level falls and real GDP rises.

key.because: a fall in the price of oil

slips.AD: Oil is an input for firms. A fall in its price lowers costs and shifts SRAS, not AD.

items.q: Consumer confidence rises sharply and households spend more. Shift the right curve and mark the new short-run equilibrium.

why.correct: More consumption shifts AD right: the price level and real GDP both rise.

slips.SRAS: Confidence changes how much households spend, which is aggregate demand. Firms' costs did not change.

items.q: How does demand-pull inflation differ from cost-push inflation in the short run?
options: With demand-pull, real GDP rises; with cost-push, real GDP falls
With demand-pull, the price level falls; with cost-push, it rises
Demand-pull comes from higher wages; cost-push from more spending
They have the same effects, but different names

why.correct: Both raise the price level. Demand-pull (AD right) raises output and lowers unemployment; cost-push (SRAS left) lowers output and raises unemployment.
options: Right: AD right raises both prices and output, SRAS left raises prices but lowers output.
Both raise the price level. The difference is what happens to output.
Switched: higher wages raise costs (cost-push); more spending is demand-pull.
Their effects on output and unemployment are opposite.

items.q: A rise in interest rates at an unchanged price level leads firms to cancel plans for new equipment. What happens in the short run?
options: SRAS shifts left: the price level rises and real GDP falls
AD shifts left: the price level falls, real GDP falls and unemployment rises
AD shifts left: the price level falls and unemployment falls
AD shifts right: firms have more cash to spend on other things

why.correct: Less investment at every price level shifts AD left: lower price level, lower real GDP, higher unemployment.
options: Investment is spending, which is AD. Firms' production costs today did not change.
Right: less investment is a negative demand shock.
Lower output means fewer jobs, so unemployment rises.
Cancelled investment is less spending, which shifts AD left.

items.q: Make it specific: explain the short-run effect of a rise in nominal wages across the economy.

why.correct: Higher wages raise firms' costs, so SRAS shifts left: the price level rises and real output falls.

specific.frame: Nominal wages rise, so firms' costs ___ and ___ shifts to the ___. The price level ___ and real output ___.
specific.model: Nominal wages rise, so firms' costs increase and SRAS shifts to the left because firms supply less at each price level. The price level rises and real output falls.

change.label: Costs
options: rise
fall

why.1: Wages are the main input cost, so higher wages raise costs.

curve.label: The curve
options: SRAS
AD

why.1: A wage is a cost for firms; it shifts supply.

direction.label: Which way
options: left
right

why.1: Higher costs mean less output supplied at each price level.

price.label: Price level
options: rises
falls

why.1: SRAS left moves the equilibrium up along AD.

output.label: Real output
options: falls
rises

why.1: Moving up and to the left along AD lowers output.

items.q: Put the chain in order, from a boom in a trading partner to unemployment in the short run.
options: Foreign incomes rise
Foreigners buy more of our exports
Net exports rise and AD shifts right
Real GDP and the price level rise
Firms hire more workers and unemployment falls

why.correct: Each link causes the next: more exports raise AD, output rises, and producing more needs more workers.

items.q: Which events would cause stagflation, a higher price level together with lower real output, in the short run? Select all that apply.
options: A sharp rise in the price of energy
A drought that ruins harvests across the country
A rise in government purchases
A fall in household wealth
A new technology that raises output per worker

why.correct: Stagflation comes from a negative supply shock: SRAS shifts left.
options: Right: higher input costs shift SRAS left.
Right: it raises food and input costs, shifting SRAS left.
More spending shifts AD right: prices and output both rise.
Less spending shifts AD left: prices and output both fall.
Higher productivity shifts SRAS right: prices fall and output rises.
